Show that $a$ is a primitive root modulo $p$ iff $-a$ has order $(p-1) / 2$.", "assumptions": [], "domain": "number_theory", "explicit_subgoals": [], "candidate_text": "Let \(m=(p-1)/2=2t+1\), so \(m\) is odd.

First suppose that \(a\) is a primitive root modulo \(p\). Then \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=p-1=2m\). Thus \((a^m)^2\equiv1\pmod p\), but \(a^m\not\equiv1\pmod p\). Since \(p\) is prime, \(a^m\equiv-1\pmod p\). Hence, because \(m\) is odd,
\[
(-a)^m=(-1)^m a^m\equiv(-1)(-1)\equiv1\pmod p.
\]
If \((-a)^n\equiv1\pmod p\), then \(a^{2n}=(-a)^{2n}\equiv1\pmod p\). Therefore \(2m\mid2n\), so \(m\mid n\). Together with \((-a)^m\equiv1\pmod p\), this proves \(\operatorname{ord}_p(-a)=m=(p-1)/2\).

Conversely, suppose \(\operatorname{ord}_p(-a)=m\), and write \(b=-a\). Since \(b^m\equiv1\pmod p\) and \(m\) is odd,
\[
a^m=(-b)^m\equiv-1\pmod p,
\]
so \(a^{2m}\equiv1\pmod p\). If \(a^n\equiv1\pmod p\), then \(b^{2n}=a^{2n}\equiv1\pmod p\), whence \(m\mid2n\). Since \(m\) is odd, \(m\mid n\); write \(n=qm\). Then
\[
1\equiv a^n=(a^m)^q\equiv(-1)^q\pmod p.
\]
As \(p\) is odd, this forces \(q\) to be even. Thus \(2m\mid n\). Since also \(a^{2m}\equiv1\pmod p\), we conclude that \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=2m=p-1\). Therefore \(a\) is a primitive root modulo \(p\)."}
